Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Train Conductor
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 44

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Silence): Sudden or complete silence, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Olfactory (Smoke): Smoke or fire smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury, Smoking: I smoke, Worst Case Rehearsal: mentally rehearse worst case scenarios to feel prepared
  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself

Vignette:
Amara is a forty-two-year-old train conductor who came to the clinic at her supervisor’s urging, after a shift during which the sudden silence of a stalled train had sent her into a shaking, disoriented state that required her to be relieved of duty. She is married, lives with her husband in a quiet apartment, and has carried the memory of being tortured for years without ever telling anyone the full story—because she cannot piece it together even for herself.

What she does recall comes in flashes: the concrete floor of a small room, the sting of smoke from a pile of burning rubber, the unbearable quiet after her captors left her alone for hours. She had been taken by militia men during a wave of violence in her home country, held for three days, beaten, burned with cigarettes, and repeatedly threatened with death. The smell of smoke, the sight of her own bloodied wrists, and the hollow silence that followed each interrogation are the fragments that remain. She cannot say how she got out, or who helped her—the middle of the narrative is a blank. When she tries to reconstruct it, she feels the terror as if she is back on that floor, her heart hammering, her skin crawling.

Amara came to the United States a decade ago, found work with the railway, and met her husband. The role of train conductor seemed manageable: predictable routes, clear protocols. But the job has become a continuous exposure to her triggers. When a passenger steps onto the platform with a bandaged arm or a visible wound, Amara’s stomach twists and she has to look away. The smell of burning leaves from trackside fires makes her chest tighten. And the most disorienting trigger of all—silence—arrives unpredictably: a train that stops between stations, the sudden hush when no one speaks, the dead quiet of an empty carriage. In those moments, the memory crashes in on her and she feels the concrete against her back, the smoke in her throat, the absence of sound as the worst kind of threat.

To manage, Amara has developed a set of routines she believes keep her safe. She constantly scans her own body—her arms, her legs, her torso—checking for any mark or sensation that might indicate she has been harmed without noticing. She smokes heavily, especially after a shift, relying on the familiar rhythm of inhaling to calm her nervous system. And she mentally rehearses worst-case scenarios: she imagines a passenger pulling a knife, a bomb on the tracks, an intruder breaking into her home. Rehearsing, she tells herself, means she will be ready. But the preparation never seems to end. At home, she lies in bed listening for footsteps in the hallway, for the creak of a door. Her husband’s sudden movements in the kitchen—a hand reaching for a cup—make her jump. She cannot let her guard down, even when she knows, intellectually, that she is safe.

Her vigilance has cost her. At work, she has snapped at commuters who move too quickly, and coworkers have noticed her startle response. She has taken to avoiding the quietest parts of the yard, preferring the noise of the depot. At home, she pushes her husband away, unable to explain why she flinches when he touches her shoulder, why she spends hours silent and watchful. The couple rarely talks about what happened; Amara has never been able to tell him a coherent account, and he has stopped asking.

Now, after the panic attack on the silent train, she has come to this office. She is afraid that talking will bring the full story into view, that she might not survive remembering it all. But she is equally afraid of another day spent monitoring every sound, every movement, every scent, and still never feeling prepared enough. She wants to find out if there is a way to live without the constant rehearsal, without the scanning, without the certainty that the next silence will destroy her.
